title: De eximio usu methodi interpolationum in serierum doctrina

deep.reconstruction:
Problem 5 (§52) seeks an odd interpolating function with prescribed values at a two-sided interrupted lattice. Write x = θω. The nodes are ω = a_0, a_1, a_2, ... = n, 1−n, 1+n, 2−n, 2+n, ... and the prescribed values are y = f, f, −f, −f, f, f, ... Euler uses a Newton divided-difference form in the variable ω²:

y/ω = A + B(ω²−a_0²) + C(ω²−a_0²)(ω²−a_1²) + ...

On this page he evaluates at successive nodes. The differences factor nicely, for example a_1²−a_0² = 1(1−2n), a_2²−a_1² = 4n = 2·2n, a_3²−a_2² = 3(1−2n) and a_3²−a_0² = 2(2−2n). This gives a triangular system whose solution has the closed form

k-th coefficient = (−1)^k f / (k! a_0 a_1 ⋯ a_k).

That is, A = f/n, B = −f/(n(1−n)), C = f/(2n(1−n)(1+n)), D = −f/(6n(1−n)(1+n)(2−n)), E = f/(24n(1−n)(1+n)(2−n)(2+n)). Since the preceding work shows the interpolant is f sin ωπ / sin nπ, he obtains the two-parameter expansion

sin ωπ / sin nπ = (ω/n) Σ_k ∏_{j=0}^{k−1} (a_j² − ω²) / ((j+1) a_{j+1}).

He gives it both with alternating signs (with Π denoting the preceding term) and in an all-positive form. He remarks that the series departs strongly from usual series because it contains two arbitrary numbers n and ω.

Corollary 1 (§53), ω→0: π/sin nπ = 1/n + n/(1(1−n)) + n(1−n)/(1·2(1+n)) + ... For n = 1/2 the terms are 2, 1, 1/12, 1/24, 3/320, 3/640, ... Each odd-indexed term is half the preceding one. Hence π = (3/2)(2 + 1/12 + 3/320 + ...). The 'posterior' series 1 + 1/24 + 3/640 + ... equals π/3, which Euler explains as arcsin(x)/x at x = 1/2.

Corollary 2 (§54), n→0: the nodes coalesce in pairs at the integers. The scheme becomes Hermite (confluent) interpolation of sin πω/π, using value 0 and slope (−1)^k at each integer k. The result is

sin ωπ/π = ω − ω³ + ω³(ω²−1)/2 − ω³(ω²−1)²/(3!·2) + ω³(ω²−1)²(ω²−4)/(4!·2·2) − ...

After division by ω, Euler splits this into the even-indexed (positive) and odd-indexed (negative) subseries.
errors: No mathematical errors found. The coefficients A–E were checked by solving the triangular system directly. The n = 1/2, ω→0 series was summed numerically: partial sum through 8 terms ≈ 3.1413, converging to π. The n→0 limit terms were also checked.
The series is written without the factor f, i.e. f = 1 is implicitly taken, although the text says y = f sin ωπ/sin nπ.
Convergence of this Newton series with non-uniform nodes (an entire function of order 1/2 in ω²) is assumed, not proved. This is typical for Euler.

ideas.what: Newton divided-difference interpolation in ω² at the two-sided interrupted lattice n, 1−n, 1+n, 2−n, ...
ideas.modern_name: Newton interpolation series with non-equidistant nodes (Nörlund-type interpolation series)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Newton; general convergence theory by Nörlund, Gelfond and others (20th c.)
ideas.where_published: E555 itself (Opuscula analytica, 1783); related interpolation work in E555's earlier sections

ideas.what: Closed form of all divided differences: k-th coefficient = (−1)^k f/(k! a_0⋯a_k), giving a two-parameter series for sin ωπ/sin nπ
ideas.modern_name: Explicit Newton-series expansion of sin(πω)/sin(πn); hypergeometric-type (well-poised-like) series in Pochhammer symbols
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler (this paper); unsure about later rediscovery

ideas.what: π/sin nπ = 1/n + n/(1−n) + n(1−n)/(2(1+n)) + ...; for n = 1/2, splitting into two series in ratio 2:1 linked to arcsin(1/2)
ideas.modern_name: Series for the reflection formula Γ(n)Γ(1−n) = π/sin nπ; arcsine series

ideas.what: n→0 limit: confluent (Hermite) interpolation of sin πω/π using values and slopes at the integers
ideas.modern_name: Hermite interpolation series; expansion in central factorial-type products
ideas.usually_credited_to: Hermite (1878) for the general confluent scheme

missed.claim: Grouping consecutive terms by pairs (a_{2m−1} = m−n, a_{2m} = m+n) turns the two-parameter series into a hypergeometric series in Pochhammer symbols (n±ω)_m, (1−n±ω)_m. Euler's closed-form sum sin ωπ/sin nπ may then be a special case of a classical well-poised summation (Dougall-type). Euler did not make this identification. Whether the later hypergeometric literature records this specific identity as Euler's is unclear to me.
missed.quote: Haec series eo maiori attentione digna videtur, quod a solita serierum ratione plurimum recedit, in eaque adeo duo numeri arbitrarii n et ω occurrunt.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It would place an Euler interpolation identity within hypergeometric summation theory and credit him with an early nontrivial two-parameter summation. This is speculative and would need verification.

deep.surprise_reason: A clean, correct, explicit two-parameter Newton-series expansion of sin ωπ/sin nπ with closed-form divided differences, plus a confluent n→0 case. It is published, but probably little noticed. Its possible hypergeometric identification is uncertain.
transcription_corrections: §53 'seu π = 2 + π/3 [?]' is a misreading. The line splits π into two series, 2 + 1/(1·2²·3) + ... (= 2π/3) and 1 + 1/(2·2²·3) + 1·3/(2·4·2⁴·5) + ... (= π/3), the latter being half the former.
§52: 'si Π iugiter denotet terminum praecedentem' (iugiter, not ingiter).
§52: the series displayed is for sin ωπ/sin nπ with f = 1; the text's 'quem iam nouimus esse' refers to f sin ωπ/sin nπ.
